description: We are aspiring team of students dedicated ourselves to technology and innovation
summary:
TerraScope is an intelligent environmental trend discovery platform developed to identify and analyse significant environmental changes in a selected geographical region using NASA Earth observation data.

Unlike traditional approaches that require users to manually select environmental variables and perform complex analysis, TerraScope automatically examines indicators such as temperature, rainfall, soil moisture, and vegetation. It uses statistical techniques, including the Mann-Kendall test, to identify increasing and decreasing trends, measure their rates of change, evaluate their significance, and rank them based on their relative strength while accounting for natural variability and false discoveries.

TerraScope addresses the challenge of making environmental data analysis more accessible, understandable, and reliable. Through interactive maps, visual charts, rankings, and simple explanations, it transforms complex scientific datasets into meaningful insights.

This project is important because understanding environmental changes at a local level can help communities, researchers, and decision-makers recognise emerging environmental patterns and make more informed decisions. By automatically discovering what is changing rather than requiring users to know what to investigate, TerraScope makes environmental monitoring more accessible to everyone.
details:
TerraScope is a website that tells anyone what is actually changing in their region, using NASA Earth science data, without needing statistics or software skills.

The user picks a city, types coordinates or clicks the map. TerraScope then automatically scans several NASA POWER variables (temperature, rainfall, soil moisture, humidity, wind speed and sunlight) for that place.

For every variable it finds whether it is increasing or decreasing and how much it changes per year (Sen’s slope). It tests whether the change is statistically significant with the Mann-Kendall test.

Because the variables have different units, each change is converted to a common scale: the total change divided by the variable’s normal year-to-year swing.

A False Discovery Rate correction then removes false alarms that appear when many variables are tested together. The variables are ranked from most to least changing.

Each result comes with a chart, a hotspot map showing where in the area the change is strongest, and a one-line plain-language explanation with Strong, Moderate or Weak evidence.

TerraScope saves guesswork by checking multiple NASA variables automatically, so users do not have to know which variables to look at. It removes the skills barrier because no special software or statistics knowledge is needed. It also separates real change from normal variation through statistical testing and reliability correction, giving users a fast and simple answer to the question, “What is actually changing in my region?”

Our goal is to make NASA Earth data useful to everyone, not only scientists. Students and teachers can learn about local climate change. Farmers can notice changes in rainfall and soil moisture. District and city planners can spot environmental trends early. Researchers can quickly find which variables are worth studying further. By making the evidence clear and easy to understand, TerraScope supports better local decisions and greater awareness of environmental change.

The project is developed using Python and the NASA POWER API (power.larc.nasa.gov), which provides free and open NASA data. The statistical methods include the Mann-Kendall test, Sen’s slope and Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate, implemented using NumPy. We use pandas and NumPy for data processing, Plotly for charts, Folium for maps and Requests to access the NASA API. The web application is built using Streamlit, with Visual Studio Code and Python 3.12 as the development environment. The project runs on a normal laptop and does not require any special hardware.

TerraScope introduces several creative features. Instead of asking users to select variables, it automatically discovers what is changing. Its “Normal Swings” scale provides a simple way to compare different variables, such as temperature and rainfall, fairly despite their different units. The TerraScope Change Index (0 to 100) provides an easy summary of how much a region is changing. This is our own metric and is not an official NASA measurement.

The “Detective’s Verdict” feature explains results through a simple, plain-language sentence rather than showing only numbers. The hotspot map identifies where changes are strongest within a selected region, while the Region Fingerprint uses a radar chart to give each place a unique change signature. The project also focuses on honest reporting by showing evidence levels instead of giving only yes-or-no answers and clearly labelling demo data.

Several important factors were considered during development. Reliability was a priority, so a False Discovery Rate correction was applied to reduce false positives when testing multiple variables. Fairness was considered by comparing variables with different units using a common scale. Simplicity for non-experts was maintained through plain-language explanations, simple evidence labels and a clean interface.

The project uses free and open NASA data, making it accessible to everyone. We also considered the limitations of the data: NASA POWER is satellite and model based, uses a relatively coarse grid, and our analysis uses yearly averages. The Mann-Kendall test assumes roughly independent yearly values.

TerraScope is designed to be scalable, with the same analysis pipeline applicable to different regions. Additional variables, such as vegetation (NDVI) and air quality from other NASA missions, can be added in the future. An offline demo mode is also included, clearly marked as simulated rather than real data, allowing the project to be demonstrated even without an internet connection.
